# My van nearly caught fire. Here’s what happened, and what I wish I’d checked.

On Wednesday, October 28, at about 2:15 in the afternoon, I was drying a Bernese mountain dog called Moose in a client’s driveway in Bedford when I smelled hot plastic.

My first thought was the dryer motor.

I had it on high. Moose is a Bernese. There was a lot of dog and a lot of damp fur, and the dryer seemed like the obvious place to start.

Then I saw smoke coming out from under the bench seat.

That’s where the batteries are.

I turned off the battery switch and got Moose out through the side door, still damp. He was honestly thrilled to be released from his appointment early. I used the extinguisher a bit. I still don’t know whether that part was necessary, but there was smoke coming out of the place where I keep a fairly substantial amount of stored electricity, and I wasn’t interested in waiting to find out.

Everyone is fine. Moose is fine. I’m fine, although “fine” involved sitting on his mum’s front steps, shaking, while she brought me a coffee.

The positive cable connection was blackened. The cable jacket had melted back about three centimetres.

My van is now off the road for at least three weeks. The repair quote is $4,200, and I’ve cancelled 31 appointments so far.

I’m writing this because Tasha is about to pay a deposit to the same person who built my van, and because a lot of the people reading this work the same way I do. We spend our days in small vans full of water, hair, electrical equipment and someone else’s beloved dog.

I trusted my build because it looked tidy.

Tidy is not the same as right.

## What was installed in my van

My van was built in spring 2025 by Darren at Coastline Van Fitouts. The electrical setup includes:

- A 3,000-watt inverter.
- Two 200Ah lithium batteries in a 12-volt system.
- A 4 AWG cable running from the battery supply to the inverter.
- A 300-amp ANL fuse.

After the incident, Priya from Sackville Marine Electric inspected it. The electrical findings below are what she explained to me and what I wrote down afterward.

I am a dog groomer, not an electrician. Please don’t use this post as instructions for rewiring your own van. My aim is to explain what was found in mine, what the numbers mean, and what I would ask a qualified professional to check.

I also want to be fair about what I can and can’t say. I’ve sent Darren three texts and an email and haven’t had a response. I don’t have his explanation to include here.

I’m naming the builder because people have asked who fitted out my van, and because someone I know is considering paying a deposit. I’m not asking anyone to contact him or pile on. These are the details of my build, my incident and the inspection afterward.

## The bit about watts and amps that I wish I’d understood sooner

The dryer pulls roughly 1,800–2,000 watts. The water heater sometimes runs as well.

The important thing is that the inverter supplies the appliances from a 12-volt battery system. A powerful appliance can mean a very large current on the battery side, even if its plug and cable look completely ordinary.

The basic calculation is:

**Watts ÷ volts = amps.**

So, ignoring losses for a moment:

- 1,800 watts ÷ 12 volts = 150 amps.
- 2,000 watts ÷ 12 volts = about 167 amps.
- 3,000 watts ÷ 12 volts = 250 amps.

Those are simplified numbers, not the full real-world demand. The inverter uses some energy itself.

For example, **if it were operating at 90% efficiency**, a 2,000-watt appliance would draw about 185 amps from a battery supply sitting at 12 volts. At a full 3,000-watt output, the same calculation gives about 278 amps.

That 90% figure is an example, not a measured efficiency for my inverter. Actual current changes with battery voltage, inverter efficiency and whatever is running at the time. Lower battery voltage means more current for the same power.

So my original note saying “150–250 amps” gives an idea of the scale, but it isn’t a reliable upper limit. With losses and additional loads, the demand can be higher.

Also, the inverter being rated at 3,000 watts doesn’t mean it constantly draws 3,000 watts. It depends on the load. And having two batteries doesn’t make the current in a shared inverter supply cable disappear.

What finally clicked for me was this: the cable under that bench wasn’t carrying some tiny amount of electricity because the system was “only 12 volts.”

It was supplying a serious load.

## What Priya found

### 1. The inverter supply cable was undersized

The cable fitted to my inverter supply was 4 AWG.

Priya told me that my 3,000-watt, 12-volt installation should have had 2/0 AWG cable for that run.

For anyone else who doesn’t spend their evenings looking at cable charts: **4 AWG and 2/0 AWG are very different sizes.** The naming system is not especially friendly to the rest of us, but 2/0 is substantially thicker.

I’m deliberately saying “for my installation,” rather than telling everyone with a 3,000-watt inverter to buy the same cable.

Cable selection also depends on the inverter manufacturer’s instructions, cable length, insulation rating, temperature, how it is routed and the protection fitted to it. A longer cable run can also create more voltage drop.

Please don’t take “fit 2/0” as a complete electrical design. Get someone qualified to check the whole arrangement.

In mine, the cable size was one of the problems Priya identified.

### 2. The positive lug had a poor crimp

The lug is the metal terminal fitted to the end of the cable.

According to Priya, the positive-end lug appeared to have been compressed with something like pliers or a hammer, rather than properly crimped with the correct tool and die.

Heat-shrink covered the connection. From the outside, it looked finished.

A poor connection can create resistance at that one spot. When a lot of current passes through it, that resistance generates heat.

The relationship is current squared, multiplied by resistance. I don’t expect anyone to remember the formula. The useful bit is that **a small amount of resistance can produce a lot of concentrated heat when the current is high.**

That helps explain why a connection can become dangerously hot even when the appliance still works.

The blackened lug and melted insulation were at that positive connection. Priya identified both the cable sizing and the termination as problems; I can’t independently tell you exactly how much each contributed.

What I can say is that a neat piece of heat-shrink is not proof of a good connection underneath it.

Please don’t cut yours open to investigate. That is a job for the person inspecting the system safely.

### 3. The fuse was a long way from the battery

My fuse was a 300A ANL fuse, mounted about 90 centimetres from the battery.

Priya said the battery-side protection should have been much closer—roughly 18 centimetres in the arrangement she was describing.

That distance matters because the section of cable between the battery and the fuse is not protected by that fuse against a fault along that section.

I’m not presenting 18 centimetres as a universal legal limit for every van. The applicable requirements, measurement method and any permitted exceptions need checking for the particular installation.

The question I wish I’d asked is much simpler:

**How much unfused positive cable is there, and how is it protected from damage?**

There’s another important point here: a fuse is not a temperature sensor.

A high-resistance connection can get dangerously hot without drawing enough current to make a large fuse open. “The fuse didn’t blow” does not mean the wiring was safe.

The fuse rating also has to be appropriate for the cable and installation. It isn’t enough to choose a big number so it won’t interrupt the dryer.

### 4. There was no smoke alarm in the working area

There was a smoke alarm in the cab, but none in the back where I work and where the batteries are installed.

I smelled the problem and then saw smoke. I’m grateful I noticed it when I did.

An alarm would not have corrected the wiring. It would have been another layer of warning.

I’m having suitable alarm provision for the working area included in the conversation before the van comes back. Placement matters in a grooming van, with moisture, hair and the conditions we work in, so that’s something to choose properly rather than just sticking any alarm anywhere.

## What the photos did—and didn’t—show

Priya put my damage photos next to thermal-camera images of her own van running a similar kind of load.

The difference was wild. Her installation barely gets warm under that load; mine had a blackened connection and melted insulation.

That comparison helped me understand what she was explaining, but it wasn’t a thermal recording of my van before the incident. It can’t tell us exactly how hot my connection got or reconstruct every stage of what happened.

I mention that because I want this to be accurate, not more dramatic than it already was.

Smoke coming out from under the battery bench was dramatic enough.

## A power-off checklist for your own van

This is a **look, record and ask questions** checklist. It is not a DIY electrical inspection, and passing it does not prove that a van is safe.

“Power off” also needs care. Turning off the inverter does not necessarily disconnect its battery cables. A battery switch may leave some circuits live. Shore power, solar and other charging sources can introduce additional supplies.

Follow your system’s documented shutdown procedure. If you don’t have one, ask a qualified professional to provide it. Don’t assume a cable is dead because a display has gone dark.

For these checks, don’t remove electrical covers, undo terminals, pull fuses, probe connections or reach into the battery compartment.

### □ Check for warning signs without disturbing anything

From safely accessible areas, look for:

- Discoloured or melted insulation.
- Scorch marks.
- Deformed fuse holders or covers.
- Cable rubbing against a sharp edge.
- Loose equipment that could move into wiring.
- Water leaks near electrical equipment.

An unexplained hot-plastic smell counts as a warning too.

If you find heat damage, don’t switch the system back on to see whether it still works. Arrange an inspection.

### □ Find your paperwork

Do you have a wiring diagram? Inverter instructions? Battery documentation? A list of cable sizes and fuse specifications?

If not, ask for them.

I want documentation that another electrician can actually use, not just an invoice saying “electrical installation.”

### □ Record cable markings that are already visible

If you can read a cable size without touching or moving anything, write it down or photograph it.

Don’t identify cable size by how chunky the outside looks. Insulation thickness varies, and a photo is not a proper sizing assessment.

Ask the electrician to check the markings against the installation and manufacturer’s requirements.

### □ Identify the isolation controls

Do you know which switch does what?

Can you reach the emergency isolation control quickly, without moving equipment? Is it clearly labelled? Do you know what remains energised after it is operated?

Those are questions I want answered in writing now.

### □ Ask where the battery fuse is

If it is safely visible, note its location and label. Otherwise, leave it alone and ask the inspector.

Have them check the distance from the battery, the unfused cable routing, the fuse rating and its suitability for the battery system.

Don’t relocate it yourself based on this post.

### □ Check alarms and the extinguisher

Test alarms according to their instructions. Check replacement dates and whether you have suitable coverage for the working area.

Check the extinguisher’s condition, service requirements and accessibility. Make sure it is properly secured but can be reached quickly.

If you don’t know which extinguisher is appropriate for your setup, get advice.

### □ Check your escape route

Can you get yourself and a dog out quickly?

Is the side door clear? Are leads accessible? Has storage gradually crept into the exit space?

This part is very much in our lane as groomers, and it matters.

### □ Book the professional check

Ask for an inspection of the battery-to-inverter circuit, including cable sizing, terminations, protection, routing and the system under its intended working loads.

You don’t need to diagnose it first. “I want to know whether this installation is safe for my dryer and heater” is a perfectly reasonable request.

## About the $40 infrared thermometer

I bought a cheap infrared thermometer at Canadian Tire for about $40.

I still think it can be a useful thing to own, but I need to put limits around that recommendation.

It reads surface temperature. It cannot see through insulation, covers or heat-shrink. Readings can be misleading on shiny metal. A normal-looking reading does not certify a cable or connection as safe.

Please don’t open an energised battery compartment, remove covers or run every appliance at once to recreate my incident.

My plan is to ask Priya whether there are any safely accessible surfaces worth monitoring once the repairs are complete, and what would warrant stopping work.

It’s an extra tool, not an electrician in a yellow plastic case.

## Tasha: before you pay that deposit

And anyone else ordering a grooming van: ask for the electrical details **in writing before paying a deposit.**

I would ask:

- What continuous loads is the system designed to run together?
- What battery-side current has been allowed for, including inverter losses?
- What cable sizes and lengths will be used?
- How do those choices meet the equipment manufacturers’ instructions?
- What fuse type and rating will protect each main circuit?
- Where will battery-side fuses be mounted?
- Are the fuses’ interrupt ratings suitable for the batteries’ available fault current?
- How will lugs be crimped, connections checked and cables supported?
- What isolation controls, alarms and emergency instructions will be provided?
- Who will inspect and test the finished installation?
- Can I arrange an independent electrical inspection before handover?

The interrupt-rating question was new to me. It concerns a fuse’s ability to safely break a fault current, not just the current number printed on it. Lithium battery installations need protection selected for the actual system.

You do not have to pretend you understand every answer. You can send the specification to an independent electrician.

A builder saying “we’ve always done it this way” would no longer be enough for me.

## What I’d do if I smelled that smell again

I’m not going to write an emergency procedure that assumes everyone’s controls and battery layout are the same.

Know your own system’s shutdown instructions before you need them.

If there is smoke, get yourself and the animals out. Operate an isolation control only if it is safe to do so without delaying escape. Don’t open a smoking battery compartment to investigate, and don’t stay inside trying to save the van.

If you suspect a fire, call 911. Don’t re-enter to check whether it has stopped.

I used my extinguisher. That is what happened, not a recommendation to approach damaged electrical equipment or a battery fire. Extinguisher use depends on the situation, having a clear escape route and knowing how to use suitable equipment.

The van is important. It is not more important than getting out.

## Where things stand now

The repair quote is $4,200 for rewiring the main runs, a new fuse block and a Class T fuse. The replacement protection still needs to be correctly selected and installed; the words “Class T” alone don’t make a system safe.

Parts are on order. I’ve been told at least three weeks.

Insurance has said maybe. The adjuster is due Thursday, so I don’t yet know what will be covered.

Thirty-one appointments have been cancelled so far. My whole income comes out of that van, and rent is due on the first. I’m scared, and I’m frustrated, and there isn’t a particularly polished way to say that.

I’m grateful to Priya for explaining things without making me feel stupid. I’m grateful to Moose’s mum for the coffee and for sitting with me while I shook. And I’m grateful that Moose’s main concern appeared to be the excellent news that his blow-dry had ended early.

Please don’t panic because you have an inverter in your van. But please don’t assume a tidy fitout means someone has checked all of this properly.

Ask for the specifications. Get an independent professional to look. You’re allowed to want evidence that the van you work in is safe.

I’ll post another update when mine is back on the road.
